articles.title: Derrite chega ao Senado após gestão na Segurança de SP marcada por alta da letalidade policial e redução de indicadores criminais | G1
articles.standfirst: Aliado do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL), Derrite obteve 30,6% dos votos. Em 2018, ele foi eleito deputado federal por São Paulo e, em 2022, reeleito.
articles.summary: Aliado do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL), Derrite obteve 30,6% dos votos. Em 2018, ele foi eleito deputado federal por São Paulo e, em 2022, reeleito.
articles.body:
O secretário da Segurança Pública de SP, Guilherme Derrite (PL), durante evento na Academia de Polícia Militar do Barro Branco, em 23/05/2025. — Foto: Pablo Jacob/GESP

Ex-capitão da Rota e aliado do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL), Guilherme Derrite (PP) foi eleito senador por São Paulo com 30,69% dos votos após uma passagem de três anos pela Secretaria da Segurança Pública marcada pelo aumento de mais de 80% das mortes decorrentes de intervenção policial, sob a defesa de uma política de linha dura contra o crime.

A outra vaga coube a André do Prado (PL). Além deles, Marcos Pontes, também do PL, completa a bancada de São Paulo no Senado.

Esta não é a primeira vez de Derrite ocupando uma cadeira no Congresso Nacional. Em 2018, foi eleito deputado federal por São Paulo e, em 2022, foi reeleito. O capitão da reserva é considerado uma das principais lideranças da chamada "bancada da bala" — formada por parlamentares ligados às forças de segurança pública e pautas de endurecimento penal.

Entre 2023 e 2025, Derrite deixou a Câmara dos Deputados para comandar a Secretaria da Segurança Pública no governo Tarcísio de Freitas ( Republicanos ). Durante os três anos como secretário, ele se licenciou duas vezes.

A segunda exoneração aconteceu em novembro de 2025, quando o secretário da Segurança Pública voltou à Câmara dos Deputados para ser relator do projeto de lei Antifacção. De olho nas eleições de 2026, Derrite não retornou mais ao cargo no governo paulista e passou a se dedicar à articulação política em Brasília. A relatoria do projeto, uma das principais propostas do Congresso na área de segurança pública, também ajudou a ampliar a projeção nacional do deputado.

No Congresso, Derrite apresentou um substitutivo ao texto enviado pelo governo e defendeu uma legislação mais dura contra organizações criminosas e milícias. Quando a proposta voltou do Senado, em fevereiro deste ano, ele recomendou que os deputados rejeitassem a maior parte das mudanças feitas pelos senadores.

A Câmara seguiu a orientação, preservando boa parte do texto construído pelos deputados sob sua relatoria. Entre os pontos mantidos está a criação do crime de “domínio social estruturado”, com penas de 20 a 40 anos. O projeto foi posteriormente sancionado e virou a Lei 15.358/2026.

Tarcísio de Freitas e Guilherme Derrite durante cerimônia de aniversário da Rota, em SP — Foto: TOMZÉ FONSECA/FUTURA PRESS/ESTADÃO CONTEÚDO

A passagem de Derrite pela Secretaria da Segurança Pública foi marcada pelo aumento da letalidade policial. Dados do Grupo de Atuação Especial da Segurança Pública e Controle Externo da Atividade Policial (Gaesp), do Ministério Público de São Paulo, mostram que o número de pessoas mortas por policiais em serviço ou de folga passou de 477 em 2022, último ano antes da gestão Tarcísio-Derrite, para 877 em 2025 — alta de 83%.

O patamar registrado em 2024 e 2025 não era visto desde 2017, no governo Geraldo Alckmin (atual vice-presidente), quando ainda não havia câmeras corporais nos uniformes dos policiais militares. O Gaesp acompanha os dados de letalidade policial desde 2017.

O aumento ocorreu em meio à defesa, por Derrite e pelo governo Tarcísio, de uma política de segurança mais dura. Logo no início da gestão, as operações da PM na Baixada Santista se tornaram um dos principais símbolos dessa estratégia.

A Operação Escudo, em 2023, e a Operação Verão, em 2024, deixaram 84 mortos, segundo dados consolidados pelo Ministério Público. Juntas, tornaram-se a segunda ação coordenada pela polícia com maior índice de mortalidade. A primeira é o massacre do Carandiru, que aconteceu em 1992 e deixou 111 detentos mortos durante uma invasão da PM.

As operações também provocaram críticas de moradores, organizações de direitos humanos e da Defensoria Pública, que apontaram denúncias de violações de direitos e tortura. O governo paulista, por outro lado, sustentou que as ações eram necessárias para combater o crime organizado e os policiais agiam em confrontos com criminosos.

Tarcísio, Flávio Bolsonaro, Guilherme Derrite e Ricardo Nunes na Marcha para Jesus — Foto: WERTHER SANTANA/ESTADÃO CONTEÚDO/ESTADÃO CONTEÚDO

Os números da série histórica da Secretaria da Segurança Pública de São Paulo (SSP), iniciada em 2001, mostram que, em 2025, o estado registrou os menores totais anuais já contabilizados para homicídios, latrocínios, roubos de carga e roubos de veículos.

Foram 2.438 homicídios no período, o menor número da série histórica. O recorde anterior era de 2.517 casos, registrado em 2024. Antes disso, a menor marca havia sido observada em 2023, com 2.605 homicídios.

No mesmo ano, o estado contabilizou 129 latrocínios, também o menor total desde o início da série. O recorde anterior de baixa era de 163 casos, registrado em 2023. Em 2024, houve 166 ocorrências.

O levantamento de 2025 também registrou 3.470 roubos de carga, o menor número da série histórica. A marca anterior mais baixa havia sido registrada em 2002, com 3.676 ocorrências. O indicador permaneceu acima desse patamar durante mais de duas décadas antes de atingir o novo recorde.

Por fim, o número de roubos de veículos também alcançou o menor nível da série. Foram 25.024 casos em 2025, superando o recorde anterior de baixa de 31.696 ocorrências, registrado em 2024.

Nascido em Sorocaba, no interior de São Paulo, Derrite ingressou aos 18 anos na Academia de Polícia Militar do Barro Branco. Formou-se em Ciências Sociais e Segurança Pública e também cursou Direito. O futuro senador começou a carreira em 2006 como tenente atuando em Osasco, na Grande São Paulo.

Depois chegou à Rota (Rondas Ostensivas Tobias de Aguiar), considerada uma das mais tradicionais tropas de elite de São Paulo, onde trabalhou entre 2010 e 2013. Foi nesse período que construiu parte da imagem de policial de linha dura que mais tarde levaria para a política.

Em 2015, uma gravação, revelada pela Ponte Jornalismo, feita quando ainda era oficial da PM veio a público e provocou uma crise na corporação. No áudio, Derrite afirmou considerar “vergonhoso” que um policial passasse cinco anos trabalhando nas ruas sem ter ao menos três ocorrências com resultado de morte de suspeitos.

A fala ocorreu durante uma discussão sobre a transferência do então tenente Rafael Telhada da Rota para outra unidade e em meio ao debate sobre medidas para reduzir a letalidade policial. Derrite chegou a ser detido pela Corregedoria da PM devido à gravação. O caso foi posteriormente arquivado pela Justiça Militar.

Após deixar a Rota, Derrite atuou na Força Tática e na formação de policiais militares. Entre 2015 e 2018 trabalhou também como oficial do Corpo de Bombeiros da Polícia Militar.

A experiência na PM se tornou posteriormente uma das marcas de sua carreira política. Ao chegar ao Congresso, Derrite passou a atuar principalmente em pautas ligadas à segurança pública e ao endurecimento penal.

André do Prado, Tarcísio de Freitas e Guilherme Derrite na urna do Morumbi — Foto: Marília Barbosa/g1

articles.summary: Carlos Viana, candidato ao Senado por Minas Gerais, votou em Belo Horizonte e destacou a importância da democracia e da tranquilidade durante as eleições.
articles.body:
O candidato ao Senado Carlos Viana (PSD) votou em escola estadual no bairro Sagrada Família, em Belo Horizonte — Foto: Imagem cedida ao g1

O candidato ao Senado por Minas Gerais Carlos Viana (PSD) votou neste domingo (4) na Escola Estadual Helena Pena, no bairro Sagrada Família, na região Leste de Belo Horizonte. Ele chegou ao local de votação por volta de 10h, acompanhado da esposa, Solange Viana.

Após votar, Viana falou sobre a importância da democracia e da tranquilidade durante a votação.

“Espero um dia de tranquilidade nas votações, que as pessoas exerçam a cidadania, escolhendo seus candidatos com toda a democracia e direito de votarem secretamente. O processo, apesar de um pouco tumultuado por agressões, é sempre um dia de muita festa para o Brasil e para a nossa democracia. Eu fico feliz de poder participar mais uma vez colocando meu nome a disposição da população de Minas Gerais”, disse.

articles.title: João Azevêdo (PSB) é eleito senador pela Paraíba  | G1
articles.standfirst: João Azevêdo (PSB) foi eleito com 32,68% dos votos.
articles.summary: João Azevêdo (PSB) foi eleito com 32,68% dos votos.
articles.body:
João Azevêdo vota em João Pessoa — Foto: Reprodução / TV Cabo Branco

João Azevêdo (PSB) foi eleito senador pela Paraíba neste domingo (4). Com 90,07% das seções apuradas, às 19h10, ele tinha 1.251.643 votos (32,68%).

Em 2026, são eleitos dois senadores em cada estado e no Distrito Federal, para renovar 54 das 81 cadeiras. Por isso, cada eleitor votou em dois candidatos diferentes.

Para João Azevêdo, este será o primeiro mandato no Senado. Natural de João Pessoa , foi secretário de Infraestrutura, Recursos Hídricos, Meio Ambiente e Ciência e Tecnologia da Paraíba antes de ser eleito governador em 2018. Em 2022, foi reeleito para o cargo.

Em 2026, João Azevêdo integrou a chapa de Lucas Ribeiro (PP), atual governador da Paraíba, e que foi vice-governador de João Azevêdo em 2022. O grupo apoiou também para senador Nabor Wanderley (Republicanos), que ficou em terceiro lugar no pleito com x%.

articles.title: Michelle Bolsonaro (PL) e Bia Kicis (PL) são eleitas senadoras pelo DF | G1
articles.standfirst: Em 2026, foram eleitos dois senadores em cada estado e no Distrito Federal, para renovar 54 das 81 cadeiras. Por isso, cada eleitor votou em dois candidatos diferentes.
articles.summary: Em 2026, foram eleitos dois senadores em cada estado e no Distrito Federal, para renovar 54 das 81 cadeiras. Por isso, cada eleitor votou em dois candidatos diferentes.
articles.body:
Michelle Bolsonaro (PL) e Bia Kicis (PL) — Foto: Divulgação

Michelle Bolsonaro ( PL ) e Bia Kicis (PL) foram eleitas senadoras pelo Distrito Federal neste domingo (4) . Com cerca de 98% das seções apuradas, Michelle tinha aproximadamente 920 mil votos (29%) , e Bia, 870 mil (27%) .

🔎 Em 2026, foram eleitos dois senadores em cada estado e no Distrito Federal, para renovar 54 das 81 cadeiras. Por isso, cada eleitor votou em dois candidatos diferentes.

Para Michelle Bolsonaro, este será o primeiro mandato no Senado . Natural de Ceilândia, no DF, a ex-primeira-dama se casou com o então deputado Jair Bolsonaro em 2007. A candidata é uma das apostas do PL para aproximar a sigla do público feminino.

Bia Kicis também se elegeu pela primeira vez para o Senado . Nascida no Rio de Janeiro e graduada em direito pela Universidade de Brasília , é advogada e foi subprocuradora-Geral do DF, cargo em que se aposentou em 2016.

Agora, eleita senadora, Bia estava em seu segundo mandato na Câmara dos Deputados. Entre 2021 e 2022, foi presidente da Comissão de Constituição e Justiça (CCJ), o principal colegiado da Casa – por onde passam quase todos os projetos em tramitação.

Bia é considerada um nome próximo da família do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro e, atualmente, é também presidente do PL no Distrito Federal.

A candidatura de Michelle Bolsonaro era dúvida no PL após discussões com o enteado e candidato à presidência Flávio Bolsonaro. À época, a ex-primeira-dama deixou a presidência do PL Mulher, que ocupava desde 2023, e chegou avaliar saída do partido.

A crise com o primogênito de Jair Bolsonaro foi considerada por Michelle Bolsonaro como "página virada" , conforme declarações feitas em agosto. Ela disse ainda ter colocado uma “pedra” sobre o assunto e questionou quem não tem problemas na família.

A deputada federal Bia Kicis oscilou entre a terceira e quarta posição nas pesquisas ao longo de toda a campanha.

Na última semana antes do primeiro turno, Bia apareceu, pela primeira vez, empatada em segundo lugar nas pesquisas com Leila do Vôlei ( PDT ) — que tentava reeleição.

Bia e Michelle formaram a "chapa pura" do PL eleita ao Senado no DF.

articles.title: An election chief lost. Then he padlocked the ballots and called the FBI.
articles.summary: REDDING, Calif. - Clint Curtis thinks something doesn’t smell right in Shasta County. Literally. As the registrar of voters for this Northern California comm...
articles.body:
An election chief lost. Then he padlocked the ballots and called the FBI.

REDDING, Calif. - Clint Curtis thinks something doesn't smell right in Shasta County. Literally.

As the registrar of voters for this Northern California community, Curtis was both election administrator and candidate this summer. After he lost, he certified the results as "full, true and correct."

He nonetheless harbored doubts. Some ballots smelled too inky, he said. Some seemed too heavy. Some felt too rough.

He stashed the ballots in a storage room, slapped a padlock on the door, ordered subordinates to destroy the keys and reported his suspicions to President Donald Trump's administration.

In another place or era, Curtis's concerns would be dismissed as kooky. But in Shasta County in 2026, they have been taken seriously enough to spur FBI agents to show up with bolt cutters so they could take a look.

For years, Shasta County has been a center of election denialism. Citing debunked conspiracy theories about voting machines, its conservative county supervisors dumped their contract with Dominion Voting Systems and toyed with counting ballots by hand. Activists sued over election practices. And during this summer's election, voters approved a measure that would require photo ID to vote, restrict mail ballots and mandate hand counts - policies that courts have blocked.

Shasta County offers a glimpse of what happens when distrust in elections takes root in a community. Across the United States, both Democrats and Republicans have seen their confidence in elections wane, especially when their side loses. In Shasta County, the doubts run so deep that some residents don't trust the results even when the candidates they back prevail.

Curtis has spent a quarter century warning about rigged elections. Last year, a majority on Shasta County's board that shared his suspicions appointed him to finish out the term of a retiring registrar of voters.

Curtis sought a full term this summer, but voters in this forested county south of Mount Shasta rejected him.

Since then, he has called the election into doubt in any way he can. He has questioned whether some ballots contained bamboo fibers, echoing a baseless claim from the 2020 election that counterfeit ballots in Arizona were shipped in from Asia.

"I have ballots that are rougher," Curtis said. "And I've been told that the bamboo fiber stuff would make it rougher. Do I know that's true? I don't know that's true."

In January, Curtis will step down so his successor can take over.

In the meantime, he has one more election to run as registrar, in November. And the doubts about voting in this county are unlikely to end even when Curtis leaves.

Curtis's backers are committed to scrutinizing past elections and remaking how future ones are conducted.

Among them is Patrick Jones, the former county supervisor most responsible for bringing Curtis to California. Jones, 58, lost his reelection bid two years ago, and he has refused to accept his defeat.

"I don't feel like - 2024 - that I lost that race," Jones said. "But then, how do you prove it, right? That's a whole other thing. How do you prove what you feel?"

Jones, a conservative activist who helps run his family's gun shop, won his 2020 race by capitalizing on anger over covid restrictions. His attention soon after shifted to how elections are run in the reliably Republican county.

He believes even his own winning race was manipulated to lower his victory margin by unknown forces. He hasn't turned up evidence, but his suspects include foreign actors, state figures, local workers or a combination of all of them.

For six years, he and his allies have looked for ways to overhaul Shasta County's elections and replace the people who run them.

They found an opening when Cathy Darling Allen retired in 2024 after nearly two decades as registrar. She had been diagnosed with heart failure, and the stress of nonstop criticism was contributing to the decline of her health, she said.

"Some local rabble-rousers decided that Trump was right and that if they don't like the result, that means the election is rigged," said Darling Allen, 57. "That is profoundly un-American and unpatriotic."

Jones wanted to give the job to Curtis, but a fellow conservative supervisor insisted on Tom Toller, a former prosecutor with his own doubts about elections. Jones agreed to hire him but soon felt betrayed because Toller said he found no signs of fraud and kept many of the county's longtime election policies.

Ten months after taking the job, Toller stepped down in April 2025 because of health problems. Jones was off the county board by then, but he and his allies saw a fresh shot to put a sufficiently skeptical official in charge of elections.

On a 3-2 vote, the supervisors hired Curtis.

Curtis came to Shasta County from Florida, and he said he moved across the country for the job because he wanted to revamp elections in a way that other communities might replicate. He had never run an election before, but he had spent more than two decades scrutinizing them after concluding that voting machines could throw off results.

He wrote computer code in 2000 to show voting machines could alter results, he said, and he took his concerns to a congressional committee led by Democrats four years later. He became an immigration attorney but also continued to focus on voting machines, both as a lawyer and as a Democratic congressional candidate.

Curtis, 68, usually wears a suit and tie, even on stiflingly hot days. A holster on his hip holds three cellphones. Because of his Baptist upbringing, he doesn't drink, smoke or curse. He avoids reading media accounts of his activity, he said, even in friendly publications.

Curtis started out as a Republican but said he became a Democrat when he grew disillusioned with the Bush family's version of the GOP. He returned to the Republican Party when Trump began transforming it.

Throughout his political conversions, one belief never changed: Cheating is rampant.

Independent reviews have found no widespread fraud in voting, by machine or otherwise. But those studies didn't satisfy Curtis, who suspects the 2016 election was rigged in Trump's favor and that the 2020 election was stolen from Trump.

As registrar of voters, Curtis sought to alleviate fears of ballot stuffing by shutting down nine of the 13 drop boxes where county residents deposit their ballots. He hired fellow election skeptics. He removed a barrier separating election observers from county workers. He decked out the observation area in U.S. flags, making it look more like a Fourth of July celebration than a government office.

His signature achievement, he said, was mounting cellphones over employee workstations to film ballots before and after they are fed into tabulators. Online viewers can conduct their own tallies and compare them with the official count, he said.

His supporters say the setup gives them more confidence in the count. His critics call it political theater, noting that some ballots aren't filmed and that the live stream has at times crashed.

Inside the office, Curtis has repeatedly clashed with longtime employees, prompting two personnel investigations. One found he probably threatened employees by saying he would throat-punch them, slap them or have them pulled out of the office by the hair. Curtis denied making such statements and has pledged to sue the county and his accusers for millions of dollars.

"These are some of the worst people on the planet, in my opinion," he said of a contingent of county employees. "And so, I will have no qualms at all about bankrupting them."

His most consequential disputes were with Joanna Francescut, the assistant registrar of voters.

Francescut cares so much about her line of work that she planned a pregnancy to ensure she could perform her duties on Election Day in 2012. (A couple of months later, a surprise special election meant she wound up working on Election Day near her due date, and she had to leave that morning to give birth to a son.)

For years, she enjoyed giving voters tours of her office and showing them how elections work, she said. Then came 2020.

After Trump lost, visitors who once thanked her came with hostile questions. She set up training sessions for election observers only to find attendees exploiting them to criticize how she did her job.

The county supervisors didn't trust her either. When they got rid of voting machines and moved toward hand counts, she told them she would need more staff and more money. They didn't believe her figures but had to abandon their plans when the state legislature passed a law requiring machine tallies.

The supervisors twice declined to appoint Francescut as the registrar of voters, passing her over for candidates who had not run elections before. When they named Curtis to the job, she announced she was running for the job in the next election.

Within weeks, Curtis fired her as his top assistant, saying he could dismiss her because she was an at-will employee. Francescut, 44, responded with a wrongful termination lawsuit that remains ongoing.

Getting passed over for the job frustrated her, but she refused to give up, she said, because she didn't want to send the wrong message to her teen daughter.

"I can't allow her to watch me get stomped on by men that are lying about me and not stand up for what's right," she said.

This June, she beat Curtis in the race for registrar of voters with 58 percent of the vote. She will take office in January.

That left Curtis with an unusually long seven-month period as a lame duck.

Curtis did not just lose the election; he lost allies. Kevin Crye, a supervisor who voted to hire Curtis, lost his own race in June. Chris Kelstrom, another supervisor who voted to hire Curtis, now says he trusts Curtis "less than gas station sushi" and accused him of creating an "HR nightmare." In August, Kelstrom joined a board majority in censuring Curtis over the personnel investigations.

Curtis said he needs help running November's election, so he offered a job to Tina Peters, a former county clerk from Colorado convicted of four felonies for allowing an outsider to copy voting machine software in an attempt to prove the 2020 election was stolen from Trump. Peters is a hero and martyr to election skeptics, and she has been touring the country to warn of rigged elections since Colorado Gov. Jared Polis (D) commuted her sentence this summer.

The job offer made national headlines and angered election officials from both parties across the country. Peters turned Curtis down, saying she wanted to keep a national focus.

Last month, after Curtis questioned the ballots, he received a grand jury subpoena telling him to bring them to Sacramento, he said. The subpoena was canceled, he said, after FBI agents and officials with the California secretary of state's office visited Shasta County to interview him and inspect the boxes of ballots.

County supervisors have called Curtis's claims about the June election frivolous and said they welcome any state or federal review of the election. The FBI declined to comment. The secretary of state's office said representatives recently went to Shasta County but declined to provide other details.

Now, Curtis is preparing to run his last election for Shasta County. His detractors are worried about how he will do his job. His backers fear Francescut will reverse the changes Curtis has made.

"We want truth, we want honesty, we want a fair and transparent election," said Rich Gallardo, a Curtis ally who has spent years deriding the county's election practices. "And we're willing to keep fighting. I don't know how much longer we can keep it up, but we're willing to fight for it."

articles.title: Trump’s opponents are planning efforts to reverse his changes to presidency
articles.summary: Democratic House members are writing bills to rein in a president’s emergency powers. Lawyers are strategizing about how to insulate the Justice Department f...
articles.body:
Trump’s opponents are planning efforts to reverse his changes to presidency

Democratic House members are writing bills to rein in a president's emergency powers. Lawyers are strategizing about how to insulate the Justice Department from presidential influence. A House measure would block a president from unilaterally remodeling the White House. Ethicists are writing rules to prevent a future first family from self-dealing.

Throughout Washington and beyond, President Donald Trump's opponents are scrambling to ensure that after he leaves office, the changes he has imposed on the presidency, and the country, will fade with him.

Whether they succeed could determine whether Trump's aggressive exercise of executive powers will be limited to a finite stretch of U.S. history or will instead become a model for every president to come.

Rep. Jamie Raskin (Maryland), the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, said that Trump's uses of presidential power can and must be reversed - but doing so will take decades.

"We have a massive reconstruction task ahead of us," Raskin said in an interview. "Fortunately, reconstruction has a great history in our country, and when it's allowed to work, it has been a lot more successful than either authoritarianism or revolution. … We will have to go department by department, subject by subject, and public purpose by public purpose to determine what we salvage and what we re-create."

From the beginning of the republic, the three branches have jostled for control over spending, war-making, immigration and virtually every other government function. Trump is hardly the first president to try to sharply elbow the other branches out of the way.

In 1981, Ronald Reagan startled critics by firing more than 11,000 air traffic controllers. George W. Bush, jolted by the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, secretly approved tactics against prisoners that many considered torture.

Barack Obama, initially critical of such actions, went on to expand presidential authority in his own right. He created the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program in 2012 by executive order, prompting GOP complaints that he was simply making up a law. He used drone strikes to target and kill suspected terrorists far from traditional battlefields. And he put numerous "czars" over areas like energy and health care, which Republicans charged was a way to avoid confirmation fights.

Tiffany Justice, executive vice president of the conservative group Heritage Action, pointed to this history to dismiss talk of post-Trump reforms, saying the president is doing nothing Democratic presidents have not done and predicting that Democrats' plans will go nowhere.

"They are full of baloney - I don't think Democrats would ever limit the power of a Democratic president," Justice said. "The idea of Democrats saving democracy, it's nonsense."

Administration officials argue that Trump has changed the country forever and followed established procedures for everything he has done. "The Trump administration has abided by all legal decisions and gone through the appellate process with great success," said a White House spokesman. "His successes on behalf of the American people will be imprinted upon the fabric of America and will be felt by every other White House that comes after him," said White House communications director Steven Cheung.

But Trump's critics say that in the scale, sweep and sheer aggressiveness of his actions - from demolishing the East Wing of the White House to pursuing legal actions against political opponents - Trump has pushed executive authority far beyond any previous modern president.

With a possible recapture of Congress just one month away, Democrats' efforts to limit the staying power of those changes are heating up.

Several lawmakers are crafting bills to curtail a president's ability to declare emergencies, which Trump has used in novel ways, declaring about a dozen emergencies to justify policies as varied as imposing tariffs, accelerating deportations and deploying the National Guard. Reps. Suzan DelBene (D-Washington) and Don Beyer (D-Virginia) have introduced a bill forbidding a president from levying tariffs under the guise of a national emergency unless Congress agrees.

Raskin has drafted bills to ban a president from accepting payments from foreign governments without Congress's consent and require a public review for renovations of the White House. Another measure would block a president from entering monetary settlements with his own government, which a federal judge scolded Trump and the Justice Department for this summer, saying they had attempted to "use" and "manipulate" the court to legitimize a deal that would have shielded Trump from IRS scrutiny and set up a nearly $1.8 billion fund for alleged victims of politicized prosecutions.

Rahm Emanuel, the former Chicago mayor and potential Democratic presidential candidate, recently released an ethics proposal for all three branches of government that would ban trading stocks and betting in prediction markets, require a blind trust for anyone worth more than $1 million, and forbid individuals from accepting foreign gifts. Trump has traded millions of dollars worth of individual stocks since taking office and famously accepted the gift of an aircraft from the Qatari government.

And Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut) has introduced a No Political Enemies Act, forbidding executive branch officials from prosecuting or punishing individuals or groups for their speech, something Trump has done relatively openly.

Some of these proposals may be partly symbolic, aimed at galvanizing voters and showing resistance to Trump rather than serving as strict blueprints for reform. Democrats themselves do not know when, if ever, they may have the public support to push them through. They have no guarantee of success; Trump survived two impeachments, prosecutions and investigations before winning the White House a second time.

Still, the Democrats say they see little alternative to trying.

The Partnership for Public Service, which trains government employees and advocates for ways to improve the public workforce, has crafted proposals to strengthen civil service protections, making it harder for future presidents to fire employees en masse as Trump and his ally Elon Musk did. Congress, for example, could strengthen rules requiring that hiring and firing must be based on merit and due process - and then confront an administration that violates those rules.

Would-be reformers argue that periods of excess in U.S. history often prompt waves of reform. The Gilded Age of the late 1800s gave way to the Progressive Era. The corruption of Watergate in the 1970s generated a slew of new ethics laws.

It is not clear whether Americans support a new wave of reform laws. But a Pew poll last year found that 78 percent of Americans had concerns about expanding presidential power.

"Throughout American history, reform follows scandal," said Michael Waldman, president of the Brennan Center for Justice at New York University, a liberal-leaning think tank that focuses on law and democracy. "It does not always follow scandal, but that's when it happens. I think there will be a real hunger, I hope from both parties, to write into law some of the protections that were assumed to be there before."

Some historians say many of Trump's actions will be hard to reverse. It is far easier to smash through guardrails, they say, than to rebuild them. Most modern presidents have expanded executive power at the expense of Congress. Whether that trend continues could depend in large part on whether the legislative branch begins to reassert itself as a counterweight to the presidency.

"Once we get through this nightmare, the rest of our careers will have to be devoted to reviving American progress and building institutions that endure and succeed," Raskin said. "That is going to be the work of the rest of our lives."

The temptation for revenge - or acquiescence

The midterm campaigns have spawned numerous Democratic candidates with sharply combative anti-Trump messages. If they win majorities in Congress, some Democrats could well be tempted to turn the president's hardball tactics against him and his followers once he leaves the scene.

A post-Trump president could, for example, prod the Justice Department to investigate his own political adversaries, as Trump has.

"It will be very tempting for Democrats to say, 'Oh, you think we are going to limit our abuse of the Justice Department? We don't want to be suckers,'" Waldman said. "But I think that would be a big mistake. Everybody benefits when the rule of law is in play across the government."

More immediately, the next administration will have to decide whether to prosecute Trump officials who may have broken the law by misusing their authority. Some Democrats, for example, say the way Justice Department officials have targeted Trump's enemies is illegal and could expose those officials to charges.

Trump, in an effort to counteract such moves, has promised that before he leaves office he will preemptively pardon anyone who has come "within 200 feet" of the Oval Office, the Wall Street Journal has reported.

Some liberals say Democrats should take a lesson from Trump on how to govern with force and purpose. Trump does not hesitate to take actions that skirt the edges of legality, happy to let the courts sort it out. He pressures private firms to back his policies. He issues sweeping executive orders rather than trying to persuade Congress to act.

"This president litigates the way he bargains: He makes some very far-out claims, not expecting to win them all, but sort of 'what the hell' - that's his theory," said William A. Galston, a former domestic policy adviser to President Bill Clinton. "If you lose cases no other president would have dreamed of bringing, and you win a few big ones, you're ahead of the game."

It may be tempting for future presidents to act the same way. "There has been an overcautiousness in some Democratic and some Republican administrations that will seem quite quaint after this administration," said Ben Olinsky, senior vice president at the Center for American Progress, a center-left think tank.

That is especially true of executive orders and actions, which Trump has refashioned as all-purpose policy and communications weapons. He has issued more than 280 so far in his second term, far outpacing his recent predecessors, according to figures compiled by the American Presidency Project at the University of California at Santa Barbara.

"A new administration will do a lot of governing through executive order," said Richard Pildes, a constitutional law professor at New York University. "They will want to show that they can act decisively."

Even while they plot a post-Trump future, many Democrats say they cannot simply return to a status quo that voters hated. Yet it is far from clear what their new agenda will be.

Max Stier, president of the nonpartisan Partnership for Public Service, said the damage Trump has inflected on the current system opens up new possibilities. Stier has suggested slashing the roughly 4,000 political appointees in the government, saying they can be unqualified and unaccountable.

"There is opportunity in this madness, the opportunity to reexamine some of the basic expectations around our government," Stier said. "Because the status quo has been disrupted, the ability to think larger and bigger is there."

Tiffany Justice, of Heritage Action, challenged that entire narrative. Trump is not wielding the presidency in some new way, she said, but rather using it as Democrats always have - and that is what truly upsets the left.

"President Trump is using his power in a way that Democrats have in the past," Justice said, citing, for example, President Joe Biden's order protecting gender transition care. "Republicans always in the past have been uneasy about using power. Democrats are never uneasy about using power."

If there is anything that gives would-be reformers hope, it is the aftermath of the Watergate scandal that brought down President Richard M. Nixon.

Nixon, like Trump, stretched presidential authority in ways that challenged the law and the Constitution. After his 1974 resignation, a previously quiescent Congress roared back to action, as lawmakers rushed to make sure Watergate could not happen again. Congress passed bills restricting a president's ability to misuse private data, spy on Americans, misspend campaign cash, declare emergencies, control spending and more.

Some critics envision a post-Trump America swept up in a similar reform fever, with lawmakers scrambling to score political points amid widespread public revulsion over Trump's self-aggrandizement and self-enrichment.

For example, Congress could make it illegal to do what Trump's firebrand housing official Bill Pulte has done - accuse the president's critics of mortgage fraud with little evidence. Or it could restrict the ability of a Federal Communications Commission chairman, like Trump's Brendan Carr, to target outlets disliked by the president.

The Justice Department is a particular focus of the would-be reformers, many of them former department lawyers frustrated by the way Trump has used DOJ to pursue his adversaries. Under Attorney General Todd Blanche, formerly Trump's personal attorney, and his predecessor Pam Bondi, many experienced attorneys have fled the department or been forced out.

Vanita Gupta, who served as associate attorney general under Biden, said Justice Department veterans of both parties are discussing how to restore the department to its former ethos of independence.

"Rebuilding will be challenging, no doubt, but former DOJ officials from Republican and Democratic administrations are already thinking about how to get it done," Gupta said. "Seasoned career leaders have told me that they would return to rebuild the department, even knowing lifetime tenure may be a thing of the past."

Historians concede the Watergate analogy has its limits. The 1974 scandal propelled Democrats to overwhelming majorities of 61-39 in the Senate and 291-144 in the House; those margins are unthinkable today. Americans have become more polarized in the past 50 years, a trend that works against any broad-based reform crusade.

A powerful executive has gained additional theoretical backing in recent decades, as conservative legal scholars have advanced a "unitary executive" theory, arguing the U.S. Constitution gives the president nearly unfettered, unreviewable control over the executive branch.

Ultimately, the shape of the post-Trump future will be determined by how Americans feel when he exits the stage: Will they applaud his exercise of power and attacks on long-standing structures? Or will they recoil?

"The president and the courts are staring at one another over the mostly supine body of the Congress of the United States, and it's very dangerous for constitutional government," Galston said.

The Supreme Court's path is unclear as well. Some Democrats privately echo a sentiment voiced by Clinton - that the justices may not give future presidents the same leeway they have accorded Trump. The court has already been far more deferential to Trump than it was to Biden, these Democrats say.

"I have a sinking suspicion if our party wins the White House in the next election, there will be a hallelujah moment and the Supreme Court will rediscover the Constitution," Clinton said on ABC's "The View" last year.

Even if some curbs on presidential power are reestablished, Trump's demonstration that they can be dismantled is likely to have long-term effects.

Young people might be less willing to work for a government whose policies vacillate wildly from one president to another, and where long tenure is not guaranteed. Foreign allies have made it clear they are far less trusting of Washington's commitments. Businesses and nonprofits could be less interested in accepting funding they fear could be abruptly withdrawn.

"It's not like a toggle switch that you can just turn it on and off," Waldman said. "Much of the federal government took a century to build."

Some historians note Trump's unique qualities, saying his combination of celebrity, aggressiveness and disregard for tradition is unlikely ever to be replicated. That suggests future presidents cannot simply repeat his performance, they say.

"Any thought that [Vice President] JD Vance or [Secretary of State] Marco Rubio gets to be president and do the same thing with the same abandon - I don't see that happening," said John Lawrence, a historian and former top aide to former House speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-California). "He has created his own unitary executive theory, and I don't know how it works outside the size and force of the personality of Donald Trump. But that doesn't mean a Republican successor wouldn't try."

In the Progressive Era, Americans took to the streets by the thousands to demand reform, Stier said, and if Trump's changes are ultimately reversed, it will be because of a similar groundswell.

"The most important question we face is whether we can return to a consensus that we had among Republicans, Democrats and independents for 140 years that an operating government of our values requires leaders committed to the public good, not the private interests of the officeholder of the day," Stier said. "Can we get back to that? I think the answer is yes. But we need a public that demands it."

articles.title: Top Republican unloads on rise of 'anti-American' candidates heading into midterms: 'You got to be kidding'
articles.summary: Tom Emmer launched a 56-district blitz by labeling Democratic candidates as "communists" and "Marxists" while rallying support for Paul LePage.
articles.body: LEWISTON, MAINE - Rep. Tom Emmer, on the first stop of a 56 district blitz across the country rallying Republican voters, spoke to Fox News Digital about what he describes as an "anti-American" sentiment in the Democratic Party and his party’s message on the economy. EL-SAYED, MAMDANI BRANDED 'HAIR TONIC SALESMEN' IN BRUTAL JAB FROM TOP HOUSE REPUBLICAN "This guy says ridiculous things like U.S. NFL football is an example of toxic masculinity, he supports a terrorist who believes that America deserved to lose 3,000 people on 9-11, and he's got this Piker guy who's just shooting his mouth off on everything anti-American," Emmer said. HOUSE CONSERVATIVES UNLEASH MULTIMILLION-DOLLAR MIDTERM BLITZ AGAINST DEM 'SOCIALIST' INSURGENCY As it defends its fragile House and Senate majorities, the GOP is fighting political history, which has traditionally seen the president's party lose congressional seats during the midterms. articles.title: ‘Phantom’ Obamacare accounts spark new crackdown as Oz targets broker fraud
articles.summary: CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz says 1.1 million Obamacare recipients lacked social security numbers as 750,000 phantom accounts are terminated.
articles.body: Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator for the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, is urging health insurers to work only with brokers who record their conversations with Obamacare applicants, escalating the Trump administration's crackdown on unauthorized enrollments that officials say have cost taxpayers billions. Vice President JD Vance announced Tuesday that the administration’s anti-fraud task force will be removing 750,000 fraudulent recipients enrolled in Obamacare, saying the move will save American taxpayers $2.2 billion. "These [Obamacare enrollees] are phantom accounts," Oz told Fox News Digital. "There are no human beings involved in these accounts. BOMBSHELL REPORT EXPOSES HEALTHCARE FRAUD SCHEMES AS TAXPAYERS LOSE UP TO $521 BILLION ANNUALLY He continued, "Why do I think that? We reached out to them. We wanted to know, have you filed any claims? We don't see anything. Have you ever responded to any questions we've asked you? Do you have a Social Security number? Without that, I can't tell if you made enough money to be on Obamacare or maybe too much to be." Oz told Fox News Digital that the administration is encouraging health insurance companies to get involved in the anti-fraud push. "From now on, we're asking insurance companies to work with brokers who record the conversations," Oz said. "Why wouldn't you?" he said. "What are you nervous about? What are you worried about? Why don't you want me to hear what you discussed?" OFFICE OF PERSONNEL MANAGEMENT UNCOVERS $500M IN FRAUD AND WASTE IN FEDERAL HEALTH BENEFITS PROGRAMS The move would help create transparency among the recipients who are applying to receive aid through Obamacare, ideally showing that the customer authorizing the transaction is verifiable and actually qualifies for the program. "I'm trying to make sure you had a real discussion to explain the policies and truly tried your best to get the right people in the right programs," Oz said about the administration’s proposal. "Otherwise, we have massive corporate fraud." Oz also told Fox News Digital the administration discovered 1.1 million people receiving benefits from Obamacare that did not have a Social Security number. "The 760,000 accounts that we terminated, we took out because the American taxpayers should not be paying fraudulent brokers to lie about people who don't exist, collect premiums and run away with the money," Oz said. VANCE TO HOST CONGRESS AT WHITE HOUSE TO DISCUSS LEGISLATIVE ACTION ON FRAUD The Treasury Department has begun handing out refund checks of $500 to roughly 1 million Americans, along with a letter from President Donald Trump slamming the Biden administration for overcharging taxpayers "to fund the operation of HealthCare.gov." "I don't know what's driving this desire to hurt our ability to regulate," Oz said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "But I can tell you, for sure, we have other tricks up our sleeve to make sure we don't let the American people get taken advantage of."

articles.title: Latino voters swing back to Democrats ahead of midterm elections: poll
articles.summary: NBC News polling shows 69% of Latino voters disapprove of Trump as Democrats hold a 24-point edge ahead of the 2026 midterm elections races.
articles.body: Latino voters are swinging away from President Donald Trump and Republicans ahead of the midterm elections, according to new polling from NBC News and Telemundo. The poll surveyed 800 registered Latino voters across the U.S. from Sept. 21-28, finding that 69% say they disapprove of Trump's performance, compared to just 27% who approve. Meanwhile, roughly 66% say Trump's deportation policies have gone too far, and 75% say Trump has mishandled the economy and cost of living, the poll found. FOX NEWS POLL: MAJORITY SAYS IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT HAS CROSSED THE LINE The poll likewise found that Democrats hold a huge advantage over the GOP among Latino voters, despite Republicans making gains with the demographic in 2024. Asked which party they would like to see in control of Congress, 59% of Latino voters said Democrats, compared to 35% who wanted Republicans. FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS Democrats had just a 12-point lead among Latino voters going into the 2024 elections, showing that Trump and the GOP have lost some of the ground they gained with the voting group. The GOP still shows drastic improvement among Latino voters over the last decade, however. In 2016 and 2018, Latino support for a GOP Congress sat at just 21% and 26% respectively. LEE CARTER: THE SUMMER POLLS MISSED THE POINT: VOTERS ARE MOVING — AND THE MIDTERMS BEGIN NBC News and Telemundo conducted the poll via phone interviews and online surveys via text message. The poll advertises a margin of error of 3.5%. The data is the latest in a series of polls showing Democrats have a large advantage over Republicans heading into the midterm elections. Trump argued at a political rally in Dayton, Ohio, on Saturday night that the bad polling numbers have failed to account for his influence on the elections. "These fake polls, they don't account for one thing. They don't account for the fact that Trump is out campaigning. They never thought this was good. They never thought this was going to happen," Trump told a cheering crowd. "With you at my side, we have always prevailed and prevailed by a lot and got record-setting votes and record-setting victory," Trump said. "We've won every battle. We've defeated every hope. We've overcome every threat. And now we are on the cusp of beating the communists, socialist, radicalized lunatics and villains once and for all. We're going to put them down once and for all." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In the House of Representatives, Democrats are projected to win 215 seats compared to 201 for the GOP, meaning the left only needs three more victories out of the 19 possible toss-up races to clinch a majority. Republicans would need to win at least 17 of those races.

articles.title: One southern state's rise is making it America's new 'economic center of gravity'
articles.summary: Jeb Hensarling says the Texas Stock Exchange is the final piece making Texas the best place to list, incorporate and headquarter a business.
articles.body: DALLAS — As companies and capital flow away from traditional financial hubs like New York and California, one southern state is making an increasingly aggressive bid to become America's next financial powerhouse. Speaking with Fox News Digital from the Texas Stock Exchange's Dallas headquarters, former Congressman Jeb Hensarling, a strategic advisor to the exchange, said Texas is already becoming "the economic center of gravity in America." "Texas is really becoming the economic center of gravity in America," Hensarling said. "As New York is increasingly shoving capital out, Texas is saying, 'You're welcome.' We put out the welcome mat, whereas New York, capital isn't really made to feel at home, and capital wants to go where it's made to feel at home." AMERICA’S NEXT ECONOMIC POWERHOUSE MAY BE RISING IN RED-STATE TERRITORY The Texas Stock Exchange, which received Securities and Exchange Commission approval last year, is designed to compete with the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq by giving companies another venue to go public and list their shares. Supporters say the exchange is the latest sign the Lone Star State is evolving from a destination for corporate relocations into a financial center capable of challenging Wall Street. "Texas has been a great place to do business for decades," Hensarling said. "But increasingly, it's a great place to headquarter your business. Over the last couple of legislative sessions, because of laws passed, it's a great place to incorporate your business. And really the last piece of that puzzle was the Texas Stock Exchange, which is now making Texas the best place to list your company and to go public." THIS STATE ISN'T JUST GROWING — ITS ECONOMY IS GETTING RICHER PER RESIDENT The exchange has already secured primary listings from companies such as Energy Transfer, Dillard's, Sunoco and Texas Capital Bank. Hensarling said backing from major financial firms such as JPMorgan and BlackRock, along with executives recruited from competing exchanges, demonstrates the venture is more than a branding exercise. "They don't put their capital in places where they think it's going to lose money," Hensarling said. "It's a lot of validation from the market already." Hensarling also dismissed criticism that "Y'all Street" is little more than a catchy slogan. "If it was gimmicky, I'm not really sure the competition would be all of a sudden setting up offices here," he said. Hensarling pointed to the exchange's financial backers, executives recruited from rival exchanges and companies that have chosen Texas as their primary listing as evidence that it has quickly become a credible competitor. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Hensarling said the exchange is simply the latest chapter in Texas' broader economic ascent. "People are coming to Texas because, again, capital is made to feel welcome," he said. "It's an economic juggernaut... all in all, they're coming here because this is where, economically, the action is."

articles.title: Neighborhood backlash collides with America's tech arms race — but is this the plan to fix it?
articles.summary: Rep. Suhas Subramanyam's four-part federal plan targets data center siting, energy costs and water use as Virginia communities push back against expansion.
articles.body: A national security push to expand the infrastructure behind America's technological ambitions is running into resistance from the communities being asked to host it, pitting Washington's race to stay ahead of China against mounting local backlash. Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., who represents America’s "Data Center Alley," warns that backlash could obstruct the very buildout Washington considers a national priority unless Congress steps in — arguing that community buy-in is necessary to keep expansion moving. "The communities are being steamrolled by the industry," Subramanyam told Fox News Digital. "They’re not feeling like anyone’s listening to them." Subramanyam is pitching a four-part federal plan aimed at breaking what he sees as a false choice between unchecked development and outright moratoriums. The proposal addresses siting, power costs, energy and water measurement, and security for the facilities and surrounding communities. TRUMP’S DATA CENTER PUSH FRACTURES CONGRESS AS LOCAL ANGER EXPLODES: 'GRASPING AT STRAWS' "If you are concerned about a race with China, when it comes to building data centers and AI, you should want to work with us on a plan to get community buy-in for where to build data centers," Subramanyam said. His Fair Share Act would push states to require large power users to cover more of the infrastructure costs needed to serve them, according to the plan. HOMEOWNERS IN THE HEART OF AMERICA’S AI BOOM ARE GETTING AN UNEXPECTED PAYOFF "At the federal level, if we say that we're going to take away some of your federal funding if you do this, then it will be a no-brainer," he said, arguing data centers should "pay their fair share for the infrastructure that needs to be built because of them." The tension surfaced again this week as Fox News Digital reported on complaints of noise and encroachment from a massive data center built against an Ashburn cul-de-sac. Subramanyam said many residents in his district understand the need for the infrastructure but object to how he says its costs and burdens are distributed. Loudoun County says data center revenue has helped it lower its real-property tax rate, from $1.145 per $100 of assessed value in 2016 to $0.805 in 2026, according to the county. But Subramanyam argued residents must weigh those benefits against costs he says can appear elsewhere, particularly on utility bills. "What's not OK is feeling like they come in, jack up utility costs and we pay for their power infrastructure," he said, also citing water, air quality and other community concerns. The industry disputes that data centers are driving higher residential power bills. The Leesburg-based Data Center Coalition has cited a recent analysis by energy consulting firm E3 that found no historical evidence that data centers increased residential electricity costs under existing rate structures. Fox News Digital reached out to the trade group, which is based in Data Center Alley, for comment on the package. Subramanyam argues infrastructure with national implications cannot continue developing "ad hoc" under a patchwork of state and local rules. CHINA ‘THROWING GASOLINE ON THE FIRE’ IN AI DATA CENTERS RACE, SAY LAWMAKERS Other pieces of the plan would establish federal standards for siting and measurement and develop protections against security threats, including attacks on critical infrastructure overseas. "I know that localities do zoning, states do energy policy and other related things, but Congress and the federal government need to get involved," Subramanyam said. AMERICA'S REDDEST STATE CHASES BILLION-DOLLAR BOOM AS OTHERS SOUR ON MASSIVE EMERGING INDUSTRY Those concerns have also become a focus of state action. Gov. Abigail Spanberger unveiled a September framework aimed at strengthening local control, shifting more infrastructure costs onto major power users and setting new standards for water use and grid reliability. "In the years before I took office, data centers came to Virginia, and the commonwealth did not have a clear or coordinated plan to address their impacts on Virginians — on their electric bills, their water, their land, their air, or their quality of life," Spanberger told Fox News Digital. Leaders across the political spectrum, from Spanberger to Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, have crafted plans and emphasized the issue’s importance on multiple fronts. Just across the Blue Ridge, West Virginia has taken a different approach, creating a microgrid program designed to attract large projects. Critics have raised concerns about limits on local government powers, while proponents have mapped out potential property tax elimination. Jefferson County stakeholders recently debated the issue with the state's data-economy liaison at a forum in Shepherdstown, where county Commissioner Cara Keys criticized the potential loss of local control while the liaison maintained that project approvals would be handled judiciously, according to WVMetroNews. "Two things can be true: You can support data centers, and you can be against the guardrails lacking in [the law]," Keys said. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER For Subramanyam, the sharply different approaches on either side of the Blue Ridge illustrate the patchwork he says Washington must address before local resistance hardens further. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The only plan I've seen is either to do nothing or a full moratorium," he said. "And to me, neither of those is a viable option moving forward."

articles.title: Rahm Emanuel urges Dems not to impeach Trump if they win the House
articles.summary: Rahm Emanuel warns Democrats against impeaching Trump if they win the House, pushing for a comprehensive ethics package instead of a "food fight."
articles.body: Former Chicago Mayor and White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel urged his fellow Democrats not to attempt to impeach President Donald Trump if they win control of the House of Representatives next month. Emanuel made the statement during a Sunday appearance on NBC News' "Meet the Press," saying Democrats should instead pursue ethics reform. "Short answer: No, because it’s not going anywhere, and it’s going to be a food fight, and it’s just going to be we return to the politics of fighting," Emanuel said when asked about impeaching Trump. HOUSE DEMS PLOT TRUMP INVESTIGATION BLITZ IF THEY SEIZE MAJORITY "You’re never going to get an impeachment," he added. "Then if you do that, you just basically prove all Washington is what the American people think. It’s Disneyland on the Potomac. Deliver the change. Deliver a comprehensive ethics package that uses the investigations to then deliver change." The statement comes as Democrats hold a significant advantage over Republicans heading into the final weeks before the midterm elections. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: DEMOCRATS FACE AN IMPEACHMENT TRACTOR BEAM THAT COULD DERAIL THEIR AFFORDABILITY MESSAGE In the House, Democrats are projected to win 215 seats compared to 201 for the GOP, meaning the left only needs three more victories out of the 19 possible toss-up races to clinch a majority. Republicans would need to win at least 17 of those races. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has declined to say whether he would support impeachment proceedings against Trump, though appeared to suggest this summer that it would not be a top priority. STEWART EXPECTS SCHUMER, JEFFRIES TO DISAPPOINT IF THE DEMS WIN BACK THE HOUSE AND SENATE "We haven’t ruled anything in or ruled anything out in terms of accountability. What we have said is that our focus is going to be to make life more affordable for the American people. We have to drive down the high cost of living," Jeffries told NBC in June when asked about impeachment. Emanuel, who served two terms as mayor of Chicago and as chief of staff for former President Barack Obama, is one of several prominent Democrats rumored to be eyeing a 2028 presidential run. RAHM EMANUEL LAYS OUT FIVE-POINT ETHICS PLAN, SAYS DEMOCRATS SHOULD LEARN FROM GOP-LED STATES ON EDUCATION Emanuel has styled himself as a moderate Democrat opposed to infiltration by the democratic socialists, but that hasn't stopped him from expressing support for far-left candidates like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. "You think people wanna support defunding the police? You think they wanna support open borders, open prisons? Run on it. I don't, and that's not the party's position," Emanuel told Fox News Digital in an interview last week. "Now, we will have healthy debate among progressive and pragmatic wing of the party. That's what a coalition party looks like. But that is it. You had a party convention!" RAHM EMANUEL WARNS ‘BERNIE BROS’ COULD SINK DEMOCRATS BY SADDLING MODERATES WITH SOCIALIST AGENDA While speaking at the Texas Tribune Festival, Emanuel didn't hesitate to praise Democratic Texas Senate nominee James Talarico, calling him "strong" and admiring Talarico for being "comfortable" about discussing his faith. But when asked by Fox News Digital moments later whether he supports El-Sayed's candidacy, Emanuel initially hedged. 2026 MIDTERMS STATE OF PLAY: KEY RACES UNFOLD AS STEVENS, EL-SAYED BATTLE IN MICHIGAN "Look, I mean, it doesn't matter what I do... it matters what the Michigan voters think," he told Fox News Digital. "And that's what's gonna determine this in this effort. And I support the Democrats winning the Senate." "So, in effect, you do hope that he wins that race for Democrats," Fox News Digital followed. articles.title: Tech powerhouse’s regulatory push bears similarities to a notorious Washington strategy
articles.summary: Anthropic's AI regulation push mirrors Sam Bankman-Fried's crypto lobbying playbook, with millions in donations and safety rhetoric critics call capture.
articles.body: Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, has pushed for greater government regulation of AI in ways that echo elements of the Washington playbook employed by convicted fraudster Sam Bankman-Fried during his time as a cryptocurrency entrepreneur, a review of public records shows. Both Anthropic and Bankman-Fried poured millions of dollars into Washington influence campaigns while publicly arguing that government rules were needed to make their respective industries safer, although the money flowed through notably different channels. Critics in both industries have accused them of using regulation to strengthen their competitive positions. Bankman-Fried’s political operation later became part of a criminal case involving illegal campaign contributions, while Anthropic’s spending has consisted of disclosed lobbying and advocacy efforts. Anthropic, for its part, denies this characterization. Bankman-Fried, meanwhile, later said his public posture on regulation was essentially "just PR" in a social media direct-message exchange published days after FTX collapsed. Anthropic has been pushing Washington to put guardrails around the fast-moving AI industry, warning that increasingly powerful models could pose serious national security and public safety risks. CEO Dario Amodei has called for mandatory testing and auditing of advanced models, while the company has spent millions lobbying policymakers and backing groups that support tougher AI rules. WHITE HOUSE MEETS AI FIRM ANTHROPIC AMID POLITICAL TENSIONS, PENTAGON DISPUTE The push comes as Anthropic is increasingly engaging with a Trump administration that has made rapid AI development and U.S. dominance in the technology a major priority, warning that falling behind could carry economic and national security consequences. Amodei joined other major tech executives at the White House on Sept. 29, where they signed a voluntary agreement outlining safety standards for companies developing powerful AI systems. Before being convicted of fraud, Bankman-Fried lobbied Washington for a regulatory system for crypto led by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, presenting it as necessary to protect customers and bring clarity to the industry. He was a prominent supporter of the Digital Commodities Consumer Protection Act (DCCPA), legislation that would have created such a framework — with campaign finance records showing that he cut checks to the bill’s sponsors in the Senate. At the time, some crypto advocates opposed the DCCPA as overly favorable to centralized exchanges such as FTX. Prosecutors later alleged that Bankman-Fried and his co-conspirators flooded the political system with tens of millions of dollars in illegal contributions as part of an effort to increase FTX’s influence in Washington and help advance favorable legislation. Bankman-Fried justified his efforts on the grounds that public safety was at stake, using similar rhetoric to that employed by Anthropic in its quest to regulate AI development. "We need regulatory oversight and customer protection," he said on social media weeks before FTX collapsed. Testifying before Congress, he argued that crypto regulation should provide "system safety and soundness." GOP LAWMAKERS SMELL SOMETHING ELSE BEHIND BIG TECH'S AI DOOMSDAY WARNINGS: 'SOMETHING ELSE GOING ON' Anthropic has also pursued a lobbying strategy that calls for government regulation, warning lawmakers that advanced AI poses serious national security and public safety risks. Amodei told the Senate Judiciary Committee in 2023 that AI poses "extraordinarily grave threats to U.S. national security" and called for a mandatory "testing and auditing regime" with the power to block deployment of models found unsafe. "Do you guys remember what Sam Bankman-Fried was doing when he was caught red-handed? Aggressively lobbying Washington to ban his competitors," Brian Chau, the founder of a news platform that leverages AI to aid in investigations, said in response to a piece written by Amodei calling for federal AI regulation. "The apple doesn't fall far from the tree." Anthropic's pro-safety rhetoric, much like Bankman-Fried’s, is backed by large amounts of cash. The firm has spent close to $7 million on lobbying efforts from 2025 through the middle of 2026, per federal disclosures, and has set aside $40 million to Public First Action, a 501(c)(4) tied to the super PAC Public First, which is being spent to advance pro-regulation talking points. "Anthropic is running a sophisticated regulatory capture strategy based on fear-mongering. It is principally responsible for the regulatory frenzy that is damaging the startup ecosystem," former Trump administration AI advisor David Sacks posted to X in October 2025, responding to Anthropic’s strategy. DAVID MARCUS: BIG TECH INVENTED AI DOOMSDAY TO DUCK REAL LIFE PROBLEMS Much like some crypto advocates argued that the Bankman-Fried-backed DCCPA would have harmed his smaller competitors, Anthropic has been accused of supporting bills, namely California’s SB 53, that allegedly would harm less established AI labs. In the face of criticism, Anthropic has maintained that its commitment to public safety is genuine and pushed back against claims that its legislative activity is disadvantageous to smaller competitors. "Some have suggested that we are somehow interested in harming the startup ecosystem. Startups are among our most important customers," Amodei wrote in October 2025, noting that SB 53 exempted companies with gross revenues below $500 million. While labs with revenue below the threshold are partially exempted, lower-income firms that use a certain amount of computational resources are still subject to transparency requirements under SB 53. Brian Chau, founder and CEO of the AI-assisted investigative publication Effort News, has also compared Anthropic’s public messaging about unreleased models to Bankman-Fried’s messaging as FTX unraveled. "I remember when FTX was going down SBF would make up a new cope narrative every week and all the FTX stans would instantly believe him," Chau wrote in response to an article about an unreleased Anthropic model. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Anthropic and representatives for Bankman-Fried did not respond to multiple requests for comment when reached by Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Cruz-Vance rivalry heats up as Texas senator suggests VP is 'feeling insecure'
articles.summary: Sen. Ted Cruz fired back at Vice President JD Vance's presidential campaign accusation, saying he is focused on helping Republicans win in the midterms.
articles.body: Sen. Ted Cruz accused Vice President JD Vance of "feeling insecure" after Vance suggested the Texas Republican was already running for president in 2028, escalating a public clash between two possible contenders for the GOP nomination. "In my experience, people engage in political bomb-throwing when they’re feeling insecure," Cruz told Politico in a phone interview Saturday, responding to Vance’s claim in an interview with NBC News that it was "really obvious" Cruz was already running for president. "So he’s welcome to make whatever comments he likes," Cruz told Politico. "I’m going to keep focusing on the midterms and helping us win on Election Day in the next 30 days." THE ONE LINE FROM JD VANCE’S GOP KEYNOTE THAT REVEALS HIS VISION FOR AMERICA Vance made the accusation in an NBC News interview on Thursday. "It is really obvious to me that, at this very moment, Ted Cruz is running for president," Vance told the outlet. "At this moment, I’m not. I’m trying to help elect Republicans. That’s what I’m going to keep on doing." Vance is considered a possible contender for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination. Cruz, who ran for the GOP nomination in 2016, has left open the possibility of another White House bid. "I’ll certainly be part of the discussion," Cruz told MS NOW in August when asked about the 2028 race. EXCLUSIVE: INSIDE VANCE'S INTIMATE CAPITOL HILL HUDDLE AS REPUBLICANS CONFRONT TOUGH MIDTERM TERRAIN Cruz told Politico on Saturday that he remains focused on helping Republicans keep control of the House and Senate in November, pointing to his campaign travel on behalf of GOP candidates in Georgia, Iowa, Nebraska, South Carolina and his home state of Ohio. He told the outlet he also plans to travel to Alaska, Florida, North Carolina and South Carolina this month. "Over the last 10 years, there’s no Republican in the country who has campaigned for more Senate candidates, more House candidates, more gubernatorial candidates than I have, and this year will be no exception," Cruz told the outlet. That campaigning has included helping Vance during his successful 2022 Senate run in Ohio. "Indeed, ironically, I spent a full day on the road with JD Vance, campaigning with him when he was running for Senate in Ohio," Cruz told Politico. "I was very glad he won that race. I was very glad to help him." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Vance has also been campaigning for Republican candidates, with appearances in Texas and Florida last week. He is scheduled to hold a rally in Alaska on Monday.

articles.title: Majority Leader Thune warns Chuck Schumer 'lives in fear' of socialists taking over Democratic Party
articles.summary: John Thune says Chuck Schumer "lives in fear" of the Democratic Party's far-left wing as Democrats block military funding and defense bills.
articles.body: Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer "lives in fear" of the Democratic Party's far-left wing Saturday on "My View with Lara Trump," arguing the longtime New York lawmaker has increasingly deferred to progressives as Republicans and Democrats head into the final stretch before the midterm elections. "I think he lives in fear of that every day. I really do," Thune said when asked whether he thinks Schumer is concerned with being overtaken by "socialists." "I look at the way that the leaders in the Senate now act, and he voted once to open up the government when they were in the process of shutting it down the first time, and it just got blown up by the far left. And then ever since then, I mean, it's kind of whatever they want. They defer to that far-left base." Thune made the remarks while discussing what he characterized as Democratic pushback in the Senate, arguing Republicans have been unable to advance several pieces of legislation that are traditionally supported by both parties, like military funding. TED CRUZ NAMES ‘MOST POWERFUL DEMOCRAT’ AS HE WARNS SOCIALIST RISE HAS PARALYZED BIPARTISANSHIP "We have a saying in my office that if you don't get national security right, the rest is conversation. You've got to protect the country. And so funding our military, the defense authorization bill, as I mentioned earlier — the Democrats blocked us from even getting on it on the floor. Historically, that's been bipartisan," Thune said. He also emphasized the importance of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, which he said is "critical to our intelligence community." "Those are the kinds of things that keep me up at night. I think, to me, it's always about keeping this country safe and secure. Since that problem is kind of now solved, people are like, 'Okay, what have you done for me lately?' And obviously, you know, we've got more to do." "But the trajectory that we are on as a country, when it comes to economic policy, national security, the border, all these issues, we are headed in the right direction," he added. SENATE DEMS DRAW RARE LINE AGAINST MUST-PASS PENTAGON BILL The South Dakota senator outlined Republicans' legislative priorities should the GOP retain control of Congress in November, which included military funding, judicial nominations, permitting reform and more. "If we can maintain the majorities in the House and the Senate, the sky's the limit," he said. Thune's remarks follow several prominent victories for Democratic socialist candidates, including recent wins in high-profile primary elections across state and local levels. In New York City, Darializa Avila Chevalier, the 32-year-old Mamdani-backed community organizer, narrowly topped incumbent Democrat Adriano Espaillat, the 71-year-old Congressional Hispanic Caucus chair and the first Dominican American elected to the U.S. House. Mamdani-endorsed state Assembly Member Claire Valdez, who won her primary in June in New York's 7th District, emphasized in her victory speech that "we haven't just won an election. We have declared that this movement is durable — that it is growing, and that it will not stop until working people are no longer asked to just build the table, no longer just offered a seat at the table, but will run the table." While progressive figures continue to push the party leftward, Schumer has trod carefully, seeking to keep the party unified under a "big tent" strategy. articles.title: Trump’s 2024 support from Hispanic voters dips in new poll
articles.summary: President Trump’s support among Hispanic voters has plummeted from 2024, according to a new poll. Just 27 percent of 800 Hispanic respondents to the NBC News/Telemundo survey approved of Trump, while 69 percent disapproved of the president. Nearly 6 in 10 Hispanic voters disapproved of Trump’s handling of border security, and almost 7 in 10…
articles.body:
President Trump’s support among Hispanic voters has plummeted from 2024, according to a new poll.

Just 27 percent of 800 Hispanic respondents to the NBC News/Telemundo survey approved of Trump, while 69 percent disapproved of the president.

Nearly 6 in 10 Hispanic voters disapproved of Trump’s handling of border security, and almost 7 in 10 disapproved of his handling of both immigration and foreign policy.

Roughly three-fourths of respondents, meanwhile, disapproved of the president’s handling of the economy, and 78 percent disapproved of his handling of the cost of living.

Annual inflation, as measured by the consumer price index, has risen from 3 percent in January 2025 to 3.4 percent last month , according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics .

Throughout his 2024 presidential campaign, Trump promised to lower prices, after inflation reached a 40-year high during former President Biden’s second year in office.

Trump capitalized on increased support from Hispanic voters and other minority groups that year, as CNN’s exit polling of 2,000-plus voters revealed 46 percent of Hispanic respondents voted for him.

But after promising to carry out mass deportations of immigrants lacking permanent legal status and doing so during the first 19-plus months of his term, Trump’s support from Hispanic voters has declined.

Two-thirds of respondents to the NBC News/Telemundo survey said the president’s immigration enforcement tactics have gone too far, while 22 percent said he has struck the right approach and roughly 1 in 10 said he has not gone far enough.

More than 8 in 10 respondents said they support deporting all immigrants who entered the U.S. illegally and have committed serious crimes, but less than 4 in 10 favored deporting every migrant lacking permanent legal status.

“Frankly, it’s the hardest job that I’ve had,” Trump said Wednesday regarding immigration enforcement . “They’ll say you’re too tough or you’re too soft. Get tougher, get softer. No matter what you do, it’s always tough.”

The rising disapproval of Trump among Hispanic voters translated to Democrats holding a 24-point edge over Republicans regarding which party respondents want to see control Congress after the midterm elections.

The poll, which NBC News and Telemundo conducted from Sept. 21-28, had a margin of error of 3.5 percentage points.
