I will bet you a soda and a nice hat that the experts are wrong. I…
articles.body:
Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) on Sunday said Republicans “have to tell the American people the truth” about the cost of living as his party heads into the midterms.

“As I’ve said before, Kristen, here’s my prediction about the elections. I will bet you a soda and a nice hat that the experts are wrong. I will think — I do think it will be close,” Kennedy told NBC News’s Kristen Welker on “Meet the Press,” discussing the upcoming midterms.

“I think the biggest issue is cost of living. I think we have to tell the American people the truth,” he added. “Telling them not to believe their own lying checkbooks is not going to work. This inflation did not originate in a vat. Started under [former] President Biden. It’s reared its ugly head under President Trump because of the war in Iran.”

The GOP is facing multiple political challenges as the midterms approach, with issues like the unpopular Iran war and tariffs. The Iran war has especially hit Americans hard at the pump, with the Strait of Hormuz — a key waterway for the oil industry — closed amid the conflict.

According to AAA, the average price of a gallon of regular gas for Americans was about $4.37 Sunday afternoon, with the same gallon of gas worth about $3.14 last year at the same time.

A recent Quinnipiac University poll found that 62 percent of respondents said they were against Trump’s handling of the economy.

In a separate Associated Press/NORC survey, 65 percent of respondents said the president’s policies were causing high prices , more than other economic drivers. More than half of respondents in the same poll also said the national economy, as well as the U.S. overall, had been worse off since Trump came back to the White House.

Kevin Hassett, the director of the National Economic Council, said Sunday he didn’t believe in recent polls that show Americans’ negative feelings surrounding the economy.

“Ahead of an election cycle, the fact that there’s, you know, possibly partisan pollsters telling us that the people are really, really depressed, it’s a classic Democrat move, and I just don’t buy it,” Hassett told CNN’s Jake Tapper on “State of the Union.”

articles.title: Hassett Disputes Accuracy of Negative Polling on Economy
articles.summary: Hassett Disputes Accuracy of Negative Polling on Economy
articles.body:
National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett disputes negative public sentiment about the economy, citing strong consumption data and retailer performance.

Hassett argues that polls showing economic pessimism are inaccurate, as people's actions, such as increased spending and low credit card defaults, indicate optimism about future incomes.

Despite polls suggesting economic concerns, Hassett asserts that GDP growth is strong and people are confident in their jobs, leading him to believe that the pollsters are wrong.

National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett insisted to CNN's "State of the Union" on Sunday that he doesn't believe in recent polls that show the public's negative feelings about the economy.

"Ahead of an election cycle, the fact that there's, you know, possibly partisan pollsters telling us that the people are really, really depressed, it's a classic Democrat move, and I just don't buy it," Hassett said.

"Because if it were true, if the polls were any value for thinking about what's going on with consumers, then we should look at the consumption data and say, Jeez, yeah, that's right. People aren't spending. But, in fact, the retailers are doing well."

Hassett added that he's often put in a double bind by the type of questions asked by opponents of the Trump administration.

"If I say, 'Oh, people are wrong, the economy's great,' then it looks like I'm insensitive. And if I then go into why the economy is great, then it looks like I'm insensitive," he said. "And so let's just unpack it and start with, well, people are saying that the economy's not great.

"It's true that the polls, which have gotten the president's success wrong every time, have been saying that people are looking a little bit depressed about the economy. But if you look at their actions, the actions speak way louder than words."

Hassett explained that "what we know from the economic literature is that, if people are worried about whether they're going to lose their job, if they're worried about whether they're going to get a pay cut, then they start reducing their consumption and increasing their savings. It's called the buffer-stock theory of savings.

"And so what we see right now is that people are really, really optimistic about the future, about their future incomes, because they're spending really, really at record levels. They're defaulting at their credit card debt at really, really low levels.

Hassett emphasized that "the consumer information data came out [this past week] that showed that consumption was up year over year at the highest rate in years. We have got GDP now for the third quarter running 4 to 5%."

He insisted that people are saying, they are confident with their jobs, and that they remained confident GDP growth was coming.

Hassett added, "And the polls are different from that. And so then the question is, Are the people wrong or the pollsters wrong? And I would say the pollsters are wrong."

articles.title: Trump takes red state midterm blitz to Nebraska as GOP frets over Senate race
articles.summary: President Trump is headed to deep-red Nebraska as Republicans ready for a close Senate race against independent Dan Osborn, who’s backed by Democrats aiming to keep the seat out of GOP hands. Incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.), who won the 2024 special election to fill out the remainder of former Sen. Ben Sasse’s (R-Neb.) term,…
articles.body:
President Trump is headed to deep-red Nebraska as Republicans ready for a close Senate race against independent Dan Osborn, who’s backed by Democrats aiming to keep the seat out of GOP hands.

Incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.), who won the 2024 special election to fill out the remainder of former Sen. Ben Sasse’s (R-Neb.) term, is still the favorite to win a full six years representing the Cornhusker State, where Republicans have dominated the congressional delegation and governor’s mansion for decades.

But Nebraska Democrats are backing Osborn, an independent who came within 7 percentage points of Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) in 2024’s race and has promised not to caucus with either party — even as the Democrats’ 2026 nominee dropped out to clear a path for him — and tight recent polling signals Republicans may be on defense in the red stronghold.

Against that backdrop, Trump is rallying for Ricketts in Grand Island, Neb., on Monday, the latest stop in a swing through red states amid an increasingly bleak midterm outlook for the GOP.

“They didn’t choose Omaha; they chose Grand Island. And that means that they are worried about this Senate race,” Nebraska Republican consultant Ryan Horn said of the president’s upcoming visit.

Though the Democratic brand is “unacceptable” to rural voters in the state, Horn argued, the close races for Senate and governor are “a testament to how hard some of the Trump policies are hitting rural America.”

Independent polling has been sparse in Nebraska’s Senate race, but a Wedgewood Polls survey last month put Ricketts up by a slim 4 points, within the margin of error, with 52 percent to Osborn’s 48 percent. A SurveyUSA poll last month put Osborn ahead by 4 points, with 46 percent to Ricketts’s 42 percent and 7 percent undecided, and several Osborn internal polls also showed a dead-heat race.

Cook Political Report shifted the race out of solid red territory to a “likely Republican” rating this spring, as Democrat Cindy Burbank declined her party’s nomination and put her weight behind Osborn . Decision Desk HQ now gives Ricketts an 81 percent chance of beating the independent, down from 87 percent in August.

Nick Puglia, press secretary for Republicans’ Senate campaign arm, shrugged off the latest numbers, arguing that Osborn “will be rejected once again.” But others think the numbers prove Democrats have a chance.

“Trump’s coming to Nebraska — it tells you that the polls that Osborn’s campaign’s been releasing all year must have some accuracy to them,” said Vince Powers, a Lincoln-based attorney and Nebraska Democratic party chair.

“I mean, coming to Grand Island, Neb., would have been like Joe Biden or Barack Obama going to San Francisco,” he added, noting that the last time a Republican president campaigned in the city was when former President George W. Bush rallied to support Ricketts for Senate and Adrian Smith for the House. Ricketts lost his bid.

A spokesperson for Osborn argued that Ricketts is “calling in all of the party boss support he can get” in light of the tight polls.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was in the state in August , and Vice President Vance stopped by in September . And outside spending has poured into Nebraska alongside other states once seen as safe for the GOP.

The Nebraska Senate race is “way more competitive than it should be,” said Kevin Smith, a political science professor at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln.

Smith described Ricketts, who won his 2024 special election by nearly 30 points , as a “pretty rock solid conservative” boasting the incumbency advantage in a state where Democrats make up just a quarter of registered voters.

“In a ruby red state like Nebraska, this should be a layup,” Smith said. “The fact that Republicans are paying attention to these places that Trump took by pretty significant margins, to me is an indication that Republicans think it’s a competitive race.”

With one month until Election Day, Trump and Vance are both blitzing through red states , raising eyebrows amid a tough midterm landscape for Republicans.

Trump stopped this past week in Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama, while his second-in-command visited Florida and on Monday heads to Alaska. The Lone Star State and the Last Frontier are host to two of the most competitive Senate races in the country this cycle.

Asked this week whether the red-state tour signals midterm trouble for the GOP, Trump did not answer directly.

“Whoever wins the presidency, Republican or Democrat, automatically does poorly in the midterms … but we shouldn’t,” Trump said, suggesting his second term is “the most consequential” presidency and touting that “we have the best military” and “the best economy.”

“The only thing we don’t have is good public relations. We don’t seem to be able to get the word across,” the president said.

Trump, who won Nebraska by more than 20 points in the 2024 presidential election, could be a motivator for voters in the state as Republicans face typical midterm headwinds.

But Trump’s approval is down nationally , driven by voter frustration over the economy, the war in Iran and his immigration crackdown. As a few Republicans in tough races start to distance themselves from the White House , some question just how helpful Trump’s red-state visits will be.

“Trump coming could certainly help motivate the base, the MAGA section of the Republican Party. It could get them fired up and help them get out to vote,” Smith said.

He argued, however, that there’s a “trade-off” to the president’s Nebraska trip too.

“It could whip up enthusiasm to vote not just amongst Democrats but amongst independents, and that might not help the Ricketts campaign,” Smith continued.

Hal Daub, a former Republican congressman for Nebraska’s 2nd District, shrugged off the concern.

“There’ll be the carpers that argue that Trump’s poll numbers are not positive, and so therefore the question will get asked: ‘Why would you bring in somebody that has those polls?’ Well, he’s not on the ballot, like he keeps saying,” Daub said.

“I think that the president stopping in Grand Island, central to Western Nebraska, message is: ‘Hey, Republicans, this is a tough race. It could be a close race. Get out of bed and go vote.’”

Powers, though, contended that Trump’s visit is coming at the “absolute worst” time for Ricketts amid a controversy stoked by a new ad from a super PAC supporting Osborn.

The 60-second spot lambasts Ricketts for casting the deciding vote to pardon a man convicted of sexual assault without contacting the victim, who narrates: “I have no idea why Sen. Ricketts chose my rapist over me.”

Asked this past week about the ad, Ricketts said it was a “terrible crime” and that he “made the best decision” he “could at the time with the information” he had, as reported by Nebraska Public Media .

But Osborn is facing his own challenges. He apologized to residents of Red Cloud, Neb., this past week after the Omaha World-Herald last month leaked audio of the independent critiquing Trump supporters for their reasoning behind supporting the president.

And Osborn — who promised not to caucus with either party if elected in November and focused on a nonpartisan, working-class pitch — also faces Ricketts’s continued efforts to brand the independent as “Democrat Dan .”

“The Democratic Party brand is pretty toxic in Nebraska outside of Omaha and Lincoln, and the Republican Party brand is looking pretty battered right now,” Smith said. “Maybe the stars align to where Osborn can really make this truly a toss-up race.”

articles.title: This Week on the Hill: Congressional recess shifts focus to midterm campaign trail
articles.summary: With both chambers of Congress out of session, lawmakers are trading the Capitol for the campaign trail as the midterm elections enter their final stretch. The shift will be especially visible this week, with a slate of high-profile debates pitting candidates from both parties on the same stage. In Iowa, Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) will…
articles.body:
With both chambers of Congress out of session, lawmakers are trading the Capitol for the campaign trail as the midterm elections enter their final stretch.

The shift will be especially visible this week, with a slate of high-profile debates pitting candidates from both parties on the same stage.

In Iowa, Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) will face off against Democratic opponent Josh Turek in a debate moderated by Iowa PBS this Wednesday. The two are running in a competitive race for the Iowa Senate seat.

The following day, former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) and Democratic progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed will meet for a U.S. Senate debate hosted by Nexstar Group affiliate WOOD-TV in Grand Rapids. The Michigan Senate race is among a handful of closely watched contests that could help determine control of the upper chamber.

President Trump is expected to continue his red states midterm tour, with a stop Monday in Nebraska, as he works to boost Republican candidates ahead of November. Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) is facing independent candidate Dan Osborn.

On the legal front, a federal judge will hold a hearing Thursday to determine whether to extend protections for CNN, MS NOW and Politico after Trump banned the outlets from White House grounds.

The judge had implemented a temporary restraining order to restore their access until the end of the day Oct. 8, but news organizations are seeking a preliminary injunction that would keep the ban blocked as their lawsuit proceeds.

Hinson and Turek take the stage in Iowa Senate debate: The debate comes as Hinson has publicly distanced herself from Trump on several issues, including the military conflict in Iran.

Rogers, El-Sayed face off in Michigan Senate debate: The Republican and Democrat will meet Thursday in Grand Rapids.

Trump campaigns for Ricketts in Nebraska: Trump is expected to make a campaign stop Monday as Republicans look to defend the Cornhusker State’s Senate seat.

Judge weighs next steps in White House media access fight: The legal battle over CNN, MS NOW and Politico’s access to the White House continues as the outlets seek to extend a temporary court order blocking the ban.

Hinson and Turek to clash on debate stage Wednesday

Hinson and Turek will face off Wednesday in what will likely be a highly watched debate as she has publicly tried to separate herself from Trump amid voter frustrations over the rising gas and grocery costs at home.

Hinson has previously called for the House to return to session “immediately” to pause diesel exports, suspend the gas tax and create a diesel relief program for farmers and truckers.

She has also argued that the military conflict in Iran needs to be brought to a “successful and immediate end” and that Iowa residents are “being squeezed” by higher costs at the pump and grocery store. A recent Marist poll found Hinson trailing Turek by 8 percentage points.

“On day one in the Senate, I’ll be ready to file legislation to make no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, and no tax on Social Security permanent. Josh Turek would repeal that middle-class tax relief on day one and raise your taxes to give benefits to illegal immigrants. Iowans won’t let that happen,” Hinson wrote on the social platform X last week.

Former President Obama endorsed Turek late last month, marking the second Senate race he has publicly weighed in on.

If Turek wins in November, he would be the first Democrat to win a Senate race in the Hawkeye State since former Sen. Tom Harkin won his final race in 2008. A Democratic presidential nominee also has not won Iowa since Obama did in 2012.

Rogers, El-Sayed to debate in Grand Rapids Thursday

The debate between Rogers and El-Sayed comes as the GOP nominee is trailing behind his Democratic opponent by several points.

A recent Suffolk University poll published in September found that 47 percent of likely Michigan voters backed El-Sayed, while 40 percent said they support Rogers in the November contest.

Additionally, El-Sayed performed better among younger voters, female voters and Black voters. Rogers held an advantage among older voters, male voters and white voters.

Decision Desk HQ’s forecast shows El-Sayed with a 67 percent probability of winning in November, with Rogers holding a 33 percent chance.

Rogers did not attend a televised debate with El-Sayed last month and said he “ never agreed ” to it, which resulted in the Democrat speaking for one hour next to an empty podium.

Rogers accused the moderator of showing bias toward El-Sayed — a claim the moderator, Fox 2 Detroit’s Roop Raj, has rejected. He requested that Rogers appear for the sake of voters.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned for El-Sayed last month, telling voters, “Remember, the Senate seat is six years. So let’s think about that in the lives of all the people that the leaders here serve, and the good work that can happen over the course of those years, because of the power and the strength of Abdul and that Senate seat.”

Rogers, meanwhile, has sought to appeal to frustrated voters by calling for an immediate end to the military conflict in Iran and a temporary embargo on diesel exports.

Trump is slated to visit Grand Island, Neb., Monday as part of his red-state tour. Last week, he visited Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Texas.

Republicans argue the stops are all a part of the party’s strategy to get as close as they can to replicating their 2024 presidential-year turnout.

But polls show voters across the board are souring on Trump’s policies, threatening Republican chances in what were once thought to be safe red states like Nebraska.

Nebraska’s Senate race has been in the spotlight as rising energy prices under the Trump administration threaten Republicans in agriculture-centric states.

In an interview with CNN’s Dana Bash last week, Ricketts acknowledged the economic reality voters in his state are facing.

“There’s no doubt that high fuel prices put a strain on the budgets for every Nebraska family,” Ricketts said. When asked about Trump’s campaign visit to Nebraska, Ricketts replied, “We welcome him.”

Judge to hold hearing on White House media ban case

A judge will hold a hearing Thursday to determine whether to indefinitely extend an order that would give CNN, MS NOW and Politico access to the White House grounds.

In a court filing last week, an attorney representing the outlets wrote that “the White House’s words and actions leave little doubt that it will immediately reinstitute a complete ban of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO if allowed the opportunity.”

The Trump administration is enforcing the ban “unpredictably and inconsistently” and causing CNN “irreparable harm,” the outlets argued.

“Moreover, the ban independently violates the First Amendment by restricting access to and use of a nonpublic forum on viewpoint-discriminatory and unreasonable terms,” the media companies’ attorney wrote, reiterating an argument he made when the outlets initially sued to regain access to the White House.

The president has consistently accused CNN and other outlets of peddling “fake news” and suggested he has a right to keep them from covering him.

Julia Manchester, Max Rego, Sarah Davis, Ryan Mancini and Dominick Mastrangelo contributed.

articles.title: Cornell case puts New York’s progressive image at odds with its rape laws
articles.summary: New York lawmakers will review sexual-assault laws, including voluntary intoxication rule at the heart of Cornell case.
articles.body:
Last month, a woman identified as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit against Cornell University, the fraternity Chi Phi and the seven fraternity members she accused of gang-raping her on the night of October 19, 2024.

Her allegations have triggered a nationwide reckoning in the United States over the prevalence of sexual assault on college campuses.

But the case has also reignited efforts to reform laws in the state of New York.

While the left-leaning state has long presented itself as a leader in women’s rights, advocates say sexual assault survivors still face pervasive legal barriers when they seek justice.

Erica Vladimer, a lawyer and founding director of Harassment-Free New York, a survivor-led nonprofit, told Al Jazeera that much of the legislation currently in the spotlight is the culmination of years, if not decades, of work.

“These are bills that we have been fighting for for years when sexual violence is not in the news,” Vladimer said.

She drew a line between the #MeToo movement, which began in 2017 as an online campaign to denounce sexual misconduct, and the current wave of outrage following Doe’s allegations.

“It speaks to the fact that the #MeToo movement is not dead. It is a movement, not a moment,” Vladimer said.

Already, leaders in Albany, the state capital, have signalled they would take action following the Cornell case.

On Wednesday, the New York Assembly announced it had formed a working group to examine the state’s sexual-assault laws and develop recommendations for the 2027 legislative session.

Still, advocates say more concrete measures are needed to address the crisis.

“I appreciate that this work is happening,” said Lindsey Boylan, a New York City Council candidate. “It doesn’t undo the fact that rape culture is pervasive in the United States and very much so alive and well in New York.”

Boylan was the first woman to publicly accuse former New York Governor Andrew Cuomo of sexual harassment in another high-profile misconduct case, back in 2020. She is among those calling for greater reform.

Here are some of the measures advocates are pushing state lawmakers to adopt or amend:

The Cornell University case has brought renewed attention to New York’s “ voluntary intoxication ” statute, a legal loophole that can make it harder to prosecute sexual assault when a person has willingly consumed alcohol or drugs.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul pledged on Friday to work with lawmakers to close the gap.

“It should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol. Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape. Period,” Hochul said.

Under the current state law, a person who voluntarily drinks or takes drugs is not considered “mentally incapacitated” during an assault, even if they become too intoxicated to consent.

That can make it harder for prosecutors to bring a sex-crime charge. The law primarily recognises incapacitation in the context of sexual assault when a person was involuntarily intoxicated, unconscious or otherwise “physically helpless”.

That distinction has become central to the Cornell case. Doe has acknowledged that she consumed substances before the alleged rape, saying that she was pressured into drinking alcohol and taking the dissociative drug ketamine.

The Tompkins County district attorney initially declined to bring charges, pointing to the law’s stance on “voluntary intoxication”. But the investigation has since been reopened, amid public pressure.

New York is one of 19 states in the US that distinguish between “voluntary” and “involuntary” intoxication when it comes to determining consent in sexual violence cases.

But the Cornell case has spurred a push to remove the distinction from the law books. Critics have argued that sexual assault is no less grievous if a victim is drunk or has chosen to take drugs.

“I mean, to have New York, a supposedly progressive state, penalise people who are sexually abused for drinking is disgusting,” Boylan told Al Jazeera.

Vladimer, for her part, explained that distinguishing between “voluntary” and “involuntary” intoxication as a means for pursuing sexual assault cases shifts the focus onto the actions of victims, rather than perpetrators.

“We essentially have codified victim-blaming by saying if you become voluntarily intoxicated and then are sexually assaulted, you essentially cannot seek justice in our court system,” Vladimer told Al Jazeera.

In June, the New York state Senate unanimously passed a bill to allow sexual assault charges regardless of whether a victim is intoxicated voluntarily or involuntarily.

But the legislation has yet to be taken up in the state Assembly.

New York’s rape-shield protections limit the use of evidence about a complainant’s sexual history and conduct in criminal proceedings. But those protections do not currently extend to civil cases.

This distinction could matter in the Cornell case because Doe filed a civil lawsuit.

Vladimer said questions about a survivor’s behaviour could come up in the discovery process of a civil case, as well as in court.

“There is the potential of her having to face questions about things like her sexual history,” Vladimer said.

Bridie Farrell, the director of victim rights advocacy and legislation at the law firm Weitz and Luxenberg, told Al Jazeera that she has seen major differences in how male and female survivors are questioned in civil cases where this practice is still permitted.

In one case involving a brother and sister who were both sexually assaulted, Farrell said the man was not questioned about his sexual history while the woman was “grilled on it”.

A bill sponsored by State Senator Liz Krueger would extend rape-shield protections to civil proceedings. The measure passed the Senate in June and is currently before the Assembly Judiciary Committee.

Advocates are also pushing for legislation to prevent retaliatory defamation lawsuits.

Boylan said she has spent more than $2m defending herself in legal proceedings connected to her accusations against Cuomo, who stepped down as New York governor in 2021.

He has repeatedly denied any allegations of wrongdoing, despite a state attorney general’s report that concluded he “engaged in conduct constituting sexual harassment”.

“Every step of the way, we have a system that penalises people for speaking up about their own harm,” Boylan said.

Boylan and Charlotte Bennett, a former aide who also accused Cuomo of sexual harassment, are proponents of the Speak Your Truth Act, which would provide legal protections for people who publicly report sexual assault, harassment or discrimination.

The bill, sponsored by Assembly member Jessica Gonzalez-Rojas, would make certain communications about sexual assault, harassment or discrimination privileged when they are made without malice.

It would also allow survivors of sexual misconduct who successfully defend themselves against a defamation lawsuit to recover legal fees and costs. The bill remains in an Assembly committee.

For Bridie Farrell, the victims’ rights advocate, the fight for legal change is personal.

Farrell was a 15-year-old competitive speed skater in 1997 when she said she was sexually abused by her 33-year-old teammate and mentor. She came forward with her story of abuse in 2013.

By then, the statute of limitations in her case had expired. Farrell later became an advocate for changes to New York’s laws, helping to pass the Child Victims Act in 2019 that extended the time available for survivors of childhood sexual abuse to pursue criminal and civil claims.

The law allowed Farrell to file her own case, which she did in 2020. She tells Al Jazeera that a trial has finally been scheduled for June 2027.

“Before we passed the Child Victims Act in 2019, New York was one of the worst in the country,” Farrell said of the situation for sexual assault survivors seeking justice.

Farrell considers the legal impediments to Doe’s case — like the “voluntary intoxication” statute — all too predictable. “I’m not surprised if we haven’t updated a law that is archaic,” she said.

Still, lawmakers have signalled willingness to reform such laws. In announcing the state Assembly’s working group on sexual-assault laws, Speaker Carl Heastie pledged to “thoughtfully” consider how the state can strengthen its laws.

“The allegations being reported out of Cornell University are truly horrifying,” Heastie said on Wednesday. “We want to do everything we can to ensure victims of sexual assault see justice served.”

But survivors and sexual violence advocates say the Cornell case points to problems that go beyond any single law. They hope to see widespread systemic and societal change.

“Changing legislation is incredibly important. But legislation in a lot of cases can only go [as far as] the paper that it’s written on,” Boylan said. “It would be amiss to orient this horrible, tragic, unacceptable, infuriating case in isolation without looking at the broader rape culture of our state and our country.”

articles.title: Trump announces members of ‘Super Intelligence Force’ to coordinate AI policy
articles.summary: President Donald Trump announced the formation of an AI task force, naming National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton to lead it.
articles.body: President Donald Trump announced the formation of an artificial intelligence task force Sunday, naming National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton to lead it. The other members of the group include Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson and Undersecretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael. The task force, Trump said, will report to him and to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles. “Following the Historic White House Accord on Super Intelligence, where the World’s most important Technology Companies came together, and confirmed their responsibilities to the American People, I am announcing the formation of the Super Intelligence Force,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. Trump on Tuesday met with tech leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Tesla CEO Elon Musk and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Clayton was also at the meeting. The summit came after AI leaders issued existential warnings surrounding the technology, which Trump has largely downplayed. Tech leaders have called on Washington to regulate the industry, which he has said he will not do. Last week, after the summit, Trump said the leaders had reached what appeared to be a nonbinding agreement of “tremendous self-regulation.” “The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government’s engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies,” Trump added to his Truth Social post Sunday. NBC News reported Friday that Trump was expected to name Clayton AI czar. Before he took over as director of national intelligence, Clayton was U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York and chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission. Venture capitalist David Sacks had been AI czar, before he had to step down when his term as a special government employee expired. Trump announced last month that he would create an AI task force as the issue has become a flashpoint in Washington and beyond, with some lawmakers calling for a laissez-faire approach, while others have advocated for action to be taken. Some politicians perceived as 2028 hopefuls, such as Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, have sought to regulate the technology at the state level.
